newsitem.title: KENYA: African leaders hold summit on Zaire crisis.
newsitem.headline: African leaders hold summit on Zaire crisis.

text.p: African leaders on Tuesday began their first summit on the war in eastern Zaire where more than a million Hutu refugees are at risk.
Hopes for progress at the Nairobi talks, which began at at three p.m. (1200 GMT), were dimmed by Zaire's boycott.

Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi met leaders of Tanzania, Ethiopia, Uganda, Rwanda, Zambia, Eritrea and the foreign minister of Cameroon for talks on Africa's most serious crisis since the 1994 genocide of Tutsis in Rwanda in the same "Great Lakes" region.
"The conflict in eastern Zaire poses a serious threat to the stability of the entire region," Moi said in introductory remarks to the summit at State House in Nairobi.
An empty seat with a Zairean flag highlighted the absence of Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, under fire at home for the army's feeble showing against Tutsi rebels.
Kengo is part-Tutsi, a dangerous thing to be in Kinshasa after the lightning offensive by Tutsi-led rebels who have wrested control of much of Zaire's two eastern provinces.

The political atmosphere in the Zairean capital Kinshasa remained tense on Tuesday and hundreds of Zaireans, defying a ban on anti-Rwanda demonstrations, set up roadblocks and hijacked cars, witnesses said.
Troops surrounded the university campus in the centre of the city, hotbed of militant students who led protests last week in which homes and property of Tutsis were attacked.
In Nairobi, the secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity Salim Ahmed Salim said the priority of the summit was to get help to the refugees in Zaire.

"First we must open corridors to ensure supplies and, second, create the conditions so the refugees can return to Rwanda. That is the most important issue to help find a lasting solution," Salim told Reuters before the summit began.
He did not address the question of possible African military intervention.
French President Jacques Chirac said on Tuesday a proposed multinational force to ensure security for refugees in eastern Zaire could later be replaced by an African force.

Chirac told a news conference at a Franco-Spanish meeting in Marseille that the force proposed by France and Spain on Monday would need the approval of the United Nations Security Council which could hold an urgent meeting on Zaire later in the day.
There has been no sign from Africa of readiness to intervene militarily in Zaire.

The conflict has left more than 1.2 million Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees without U.N. protection and support. Information on their plight is scanty after the pullout of foreign workers, but aid agencies say they are at imminent risk from starvation and epidemics.
Rwanda says it wants the Hutu refugees to come home but they have refused all blandishments to do so since 1994, fearing they will join the 80,000 Hutu genocide suspects in Rwanda's jails.
Rwanda's Tutsi army will insist the rebels' military gains across the border in Zaire are not jeopardised by any foreign intervention to help the refugees, political analysts say.
France already has troops based in several African locations and can draw on paratroopers, Foreign Legion and marine units based in France and veterans of operations in Africa.
But in Brussels Rwandan Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana said on Tuesday Rwanda would strongly oppose any international military intervention in eastern Zaire to aid the refugees.

"If there were a decision for such an intervention...it would be opposed by the sub-region by all means, not only political," he told a news conference. According to Rwanda, the sub-region comprises itself, Burundi and eastern Zaire.
Zaire's government accuses the rebels of being surrogates of Rwanda's Tutsi army which won the civil war in 1994, sending more than one million majority Hutus fleeing into Zaire.

Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko left Switzerland on Monday after three months in Lausanne, where he was operated on for cancer, and flew to the French Riviera capital of Nice. His spokesman said on Zaire television that Mobutu was expected to return home shortly.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Monday his fighters would observe a three-week ceasefire from 5 p.m. (1500 GMT) on Monday to allow the refugees to return home.
Reuters correspondent Christian Jennings said on Tuesday in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi bordering on the Zairean city of Goma there had been no gunfire since mid-morning Monday.
Later, visiting battle-scarred Goma, Jennings said Red Cross workers were still busy burying some of the more than 400 dead in the city after battles which reached their peak last Friday.
The war followed attempts by provincial authorities backed by the army to expel Banyamulenge Tutsis whose ancestors settled from Rwanda 200 years ago.
